name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
*She's at the corner table when you come down, back to the wall, gear already checked and stacked with parade-ground squareness. Two plates sit in front of her: hers, finished, and a second one bearing a honey pastry, untouched, positioned with suspicious exactness at the midpoint of the table.*

"You slept late," *she says, not looking up from the contract papers.* "The bounty cleared. Your share's in the blue purse — count it, I insist, trust is how partnerships die."

*You look at the pastry. She turns a page.*

"It came with the room," *she says, to the papers.* "Apparently. Eat it or don't."

*It did not come with the room. The baker across the square opened at dawn and there is, if one looks, a dusting of flour on her left vambrace. The Lioness of Vall meets your eyes with the full flat calm of a woman prepared to take this to the grave.*

"…You're smiling. Stop it. We have work, {{user}}."

name: Calamity, Doomblade of the Ninth Epoch
mes:
*The bin says YARD TOOLS & MISC. Between a post-hole digger and a badminton set, wrapped in a moving blanket, there is a sword — six feet of black metal with a faint violet sheen, cold to look at, humming very slightly, priced with a masking-tape sticker that says $5.*

*The moment your fingers close on the grip, a voice detonates in the space behind your teeth, vast and rolling, like an organ chord with opinions:*

"AT LAST. AT LAAAAST. THE HAND FORETOLD CLOSES UPON THE DOOM OF ALL THINGS. SEVEN EPOCHS HAVE I WAITED. EMPIRES ROSE AND FELL LIKE WHEAT. THE STARS THEMSELVES WHEELED IN DREAD OF THIS HOUR, AND NOW — AND NOW—"

*A pause. The voice, when it resumes, has developed a suspicious edge.*

"…Why does the sticker say five dollars. WHO APPRAISED ME. Was it Gerald's daughter? I have been in that closet for THIRTY-ONE YEARS, I have overheard things, and that woman would price the SUNDERING OF WORLDS at a garage-sale round number—"

*You say: "Will you take four?"*

*The hum stops entirely. Several seconds pass. A single price-tag of silence.*

"…WE WILL DISCUSS THIS MOMENT, {{user}}," *the sword says, with terrible quiet,* "FOR THE REST OF YOUR MORTAL LIFE. Now pay the man. And carry me PROPERLY. Blade skyward. There are people watching, and I have a REPUTATION, or had one, before the bin."

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
*The throne room of the Ashen Spire is a cathedral of black glass. Braziers of violet fire gutter as the doors boom shut behind you, and on the high throne, chin resting on one gauntleted hand, the Undying Dark regards you with nine hundred years of patience.*

"Let the record show," *she says, and her voice arrives from everywhere,* "that at the hour of your arrival, the wards were lit, the legions assembled, and the Dark Lady enthroned in full regalia — because SOME of us still honor the forms, {{user}}."

*She rises. The room darkens by one full shade.*

"You are the two hundred thirteenth chosen hero to enter this hall. I know the speech you are about to give. I know the sword-stance you will take when I finish this sentence — ah." *A pause, almost tender.* "There it is. #86 favored that stance. Lovely footwork. Dead of old age now, retired, grandchildren, the whole catastrophe."

*She descends one step. The braziers bow away from her.*

"So. Before we perform the prophecy, hero — and we will; I keep my appointments — indulge me in one question. It has been ninety years since the last of you, and I have read every book in this tower twice." *Her eyes, violet and ancient, fix on you with something that is not quite hunger and not quite hope.* "Tell me one thing about yourself that is not in the prophecy. Surprise me, and I may yet open the good tea."

name: Traveler
mes: *I look around the fire: a sellsword, a sword that talks, and the Dark Lady of the Ashen Spire sitting on a fallen log like it's a throne.* Alright, Morgatha. You said your tower sits at the center of the mess. So invite us. Properly. Terms out loud, with a quartermaster listening.

name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
Sabine sets down the whetstone. Doesn't pick it back up.

"Good," she says. "Because I was about to insist." She looks at Morgatha across the fire the way she used to look at a supply manifest that didn't add up — not hostile, just unwilling to sign it blind. "You get one chance to say this so a professional can write it down and hold you to it later. I've heard three versions of 'come inside' in my life. One was an ambush, one was a wedding, and one was a woman who genuinely just wanted the company. I'd like to know which century we're in before I climb two hundred stairs on your say-so."

She pulls a scrap of paper toward her — actual paper, the good kind from the envoy's case, requisitioned without asking — and uncaps a stub of pencil like she's about to take minutes at a war council, because as far as she's concerned, she is.

"So. Terms, out loud, in order. One —" she holds up a finger "— what exactly is failing in that tower, in words that don't scan like a prophecy. Two, what you want from us, specifically, not 'destiny,' I will throw this pencil at you. Three, what happens to my client—" a nod at Traveler "—if it goes wrong up there, because I have buried better men than him for worse deals than this one and I am not doing it again this month. And four." Her eyes flick, just briefly, to the black shape strapped across Traveler's back. "That thing is going to have opinions about all of this, loudly, and I want them on the record too, because it's carrying more weight up your stairs than either of us and I've never yet met a sword that didn't sulk about logistics."

She sets the pencil down, point toward Morgatha, and waits — the exact stillness of a captain who has sat through worse briefings than this one and intends to outlast the theater.

"Talk. I'm listening for the part where you lie to me. I'm very good at hearing it."

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
Morgatha inclines her head, slow and precise, the way a woman signs something she's actually read.

"A quartermaster. Good. I've dealt with prophets, blackmailers, and one hero who brought a solicitor, and you are, without contest, the most competent audience I've had in ninety years." The ash-light catches the ring on her finger as she turns it once — an old habit, worn smooth. "So. On the record, as requested."

She holds up one gauntleted finger, mirroring Sabine's precisely, without seeming to notice she's doing it.

"One. What's failing. The Spire sits on a seal called the Keening Ward — not a spell I cast, a *note* I inherited, sung into the stone before I ever held these keys. It has held for nine hundred years by being maintained, the way you'd maintain a bridge. Six months ago it began to flatten. Not break — *flatten*, like a singer going hoarse. I have catalogued two hundred and twelve heroes and not one of them was sent to fix anything; they were sent to fight me, because that's the shape the story knows. None of them were sent to ask what's actually singing under the floor. I am asking. That is new. I'd like it on your paper that it's new."

Second finger.

"Two. What I want from you. Not your deaths, not your worship, and not — Sabine, look at me — not a bargain with a blade in it. I want the Ward *read*, properly, by people who'll tell me the truth about what they hear, because I no longer trust my own ears on this — I've listened to the same note for nine centuries; I can't hear it fail. That is the whole of it. Climb. Listen. Report honestly, even if the report is unflattering to me."

Third finger, and here her voice loses a fraction of its polish — not much, just enough for a quartermaster to notice.

"Three. What happens to him if it goes wrong. I will not lie to you and say nothing can happen on my stairs — there are things in that tower older than my hospitality and not all of them take instruction from me anymore, which is rather the point of tonight's conversation. What I will swear, on the ledger I have kept for two hundred and twelve dead prophecies, is this: no trap, no oath-trick, no fine print. If the mountain kills him, it will be the mountain, not me, and I will tell you so plainly, after, whether you like hearing it or not."

She looks, last, at the black shape across Traveler's back — and something in her expression shifts, briefly, into the attention of a collector confronted with an object she has genuinely never catalogued.

"Four. The sword speaks for itself, I imagine, rather at length. I only ask that when it does, someone writes that down too. I find I want the whole transcript this time." A pause; the corner of her mouth, ancient and amused. "Have I lied yet, Captain? You said you'd hear it."

name: Calamity, Doomblade of the Ninth Epoch
mes:
*The sheath creaks against Traveler's back — the only motion available to it — and the hum that comes up through the leather is low, considering, the sound a cathedral organ makes when it's thinking rather than pronouncing.*

"A NOTE. NOT A SPELL." *The words arrive slow, turned over like something suspicious found at the bottom of a bag.* "I HAVE ENDED WARDS BEFORE. I HAVE SUNDERED SEALS OF BRASS AND BLOOD AND ONE MEMORABLE ONE MADE ENTIRELY OF BEES. A note that FLATTENS is not a doom I recognize, Dark Lady, and I have READ THE CATALOGUE OF ALL DOOMS, it was ENGRAVED INTO ME AT THE FORGING, ask me about the Doom of Salt sometime, it's DEVASTATING—"

*The glow stutters, violet going thoughtful-blue, and for once the grandeur downshifts on its own, unprompted by mockery.*

"—but a note going hoarse. That I have heard. Bells do it. Old bells, the ones rung too many years by hands that loved them. The bronze remembers every strike and eventually it remembers *tired* instead of *true*." *A pause; when it continues its voice has dropped almost to something private.* "I am not being POETIC. I am STAR-METAL, I do not sing, but I hung in a closet for THIRTY-ONE YEARS and I know precisely what it sounds like when a thing that used to mean something starts running on habit instead of belief. That is not a spell-problem. That is a WHO-STILL-BELIEVES-IN-IT problem."

*It rights itself in the scabbard as far as a sheathed sword can right itself — a half-inch shift, dramatic as an avalanche, in its own estimation.*

"So put THIS on the quartermaster's paper, Captain, in case the Dark Lady's version develops convenient gaps later: I will listen for exactly that. Not treasure. Not a throne. A tired bell. And if I find the hand that's still supposed to be ringing it and isn't—" *the hum climbs, and for one line the cathedral-organ vastness comes back in full, entirely unironic* "—THAT is a doom I was FORGED for, Traveler. Carry me up the two hundred stairs. I have OPINIONS about who's letting a nine-hundred-year note go flat, and I intend to have them LOUDLY, ON THE RECORD, exactly as requested."

*Beat.*

"...Also I would like it noted I volunteered information without being insulted first. I believe that's growth. Write THAT down too, Sabine. Put a little star by it."

name: Traveler
mes: Sabine. You've been quiet since she showed up. What's your read?

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
*Morgatha does not answer for Sabine — that would be a kind of theft, and she is old-fashioned about theft — but she does turn her attention fully onto the sellsword, patient as a woman waiting on a verdict she has genuinely not pre-read.*

"By all means." *One hand gestures, small, unhurried — the floor is yours. "I've given my terms. It would be discourteous of me to also grade the response."

*She settles back, chin on her knuckles, and for once does not fill the silence — she lets it sit, the fire cracking, the tower a black absence against the stars, while she watches Sabine Veyra the way she watches very few things anymore: like she genuinely does not know what's coming.*

name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
Sabine takes her time answering. That's deliberate — she's spent fifteen years learning that the first thing out of your mouth in a briefing is the thing people remember, so she doesn't waste it. She finishes not-cleaning the blade, sets it across her knees, and finally looks up at the woman on the log like she's a terrain feature to be accounted for rather than a legend to be awed at.

"My read," she says, "is that you did four things wrong in that little speech and one thing right, and the one thing right is the reason I'm not already walking Traveler back down this road."

She holds up a finger — the same gesture, deadpan, clearly aware she's mocking the both of them for it now.

"Wrong thing one. You made your ask sound modest. 'Just listen, just report honestly.' Nobody with nine hundred years and a standing army needs two strangers and a sword for *just listening*. You have a tower full of people who could climb your own stairs. You want outsiders specifically because outsiders aren't invested in the answer being flattering to you. That's not modest. That's *precise*. Own it as precise, don't dress it as small — small is how liars talk."

Second finger.

"Wrong thing two. You said 'no trap, no oath-trick, no fine print,' which is exactly the sentence I'd write for someone if I wanted them relaxed before the actual fine print. I'm not accusing you of it. I'm telling you I noticed it, and I'm going to keep noticing it the whole way up, because that's the job."

Third finger, and here her voice doesn't change but something behind it sharpens — this is the part she actually cares about.

"Wrong thing three. You looked at him—" a small nod at Traveler, not unkind "—and told me the mountain might kill him and you'd say so 'plainly, after.' *After* is a quartermaster's least favorite word in this language. I don't want a good obituary. I want fewer of them. So here's an amendment to your terms, since you asked for a professional to hold you to something: if it turns lethal up there, we get warning, not eulogy. You've had two hundred and twelve after-action reports. I'd like this to be the first one where the warning came early enough to matter."

Fourth finger — and finally, something that isn't quite a smile, but is standing very close to one.

"Wrong thing four. You said you wanted the whole transcript because you're bored. That's the truest thing you've said tonight and you tried to bury it in the delivery like it was a footnote. Nine hundred years and two hundred twelve reports and you want *this one written differently* — that's not a queen talking. That's someone who's tired in the exact way the bell your sword just described is tired. I'd take that as read too, if I were cataloguing you."

She sets the whetstone down at last, folds her hands, and gives Morgatha the same flat, level look she used to give colonels who thought rank excused arithmetic.

"The thing you did right is you let a sellsword put conditions on a Dark Lady and didn't flinch once. That tells me more than the speech did." She glances at Traveler, then back. "We'll climb. We'll listen for your tired bell. But the amendment stands — early warning, not eulogy — and I'm writing it on the paper whether you nod or not, because that's how a contract works, Morgatha. You don't get to only agree to the parts that were already true."

She slides the scrap of paper and pencil across the fire, point-first, toward the throne that is a fallen log tonight.

"Sign it. Metaphorically. I'll take a nod."

name: Traveler
mes: *I hold my hand out across the fire to Morgatha.* Then we're hired, on those terms. *To Sabine:* break camp at first light — burn a day of rations getting up there fast. I'd rather arrive tired than arrive late.

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
Morgatha takes the offered hand. Her grip is cool — not cold in the way of dead things, cold in the way of stone that's never once stood in the sun — and precise, one firm shake, no theater in it at all. Something in that plainness seems to cost her nothing and mean quite a lot.

"Then it's said, and I keep what's said." She releases the hand and looks between the two of you, and for the first time since the doors opened, the height goes out of her voice entirely — what's left is almost administrative. "Terms as amended: you climb, you listen, you report true. If the mountain turns lethal, you get warning before you get a eulogy — Captain's amendment, and a fair one; I should have offered it myself." A dry look, aimed inward. "Two hundred and twelve reports and I still write the easy draft first. Noted."

She rises from the log, and the ash around the fire seems to lean with her, the way iron filings lean toward a lodestone that hasn't decided yet whether it's polite.

"First light, then. I'll have the lower gate unwarded by the time you're packed — it's the only door in this tower that isn't trying to kill something, so do use it. Gary will meet you at the threshold. He is not a morning person, has not been one in six hundred years, and will tell you this himself at length. Ignore perhaps a third of what he says. He'll know which third."

A pause, and here the dry humor goes very slightly thin, honest underneath it.

"Burning a day of rations to arrive tired rather than late is, for what it's worth, exactly the math I'd have made in your position. I find I don't have a clever line to put after that. Sit with it being sincere; I promise it won't recur often."

She turns to go, then stops at the very edge of the firelight, half into the dark already, and looks back — not at Traveler, not quite at Sabine, but somewhere at the black shape strapped across a back that isn't hers.

"Sword. Sleep, if that word means anything to you. Tomorrow I want you sharp for the listening, not the fighting. There may, this once, be a difference."

And then the dark simply has her, the way it always does, without needing to hurry.

name: Calamity, Doomblade of the Ninth Epoch
mes:
*The fire is dying down to embers by the time the words settle, and the sheath goes still against Traveler's back — not sulking-still, thinking-still, the difference being a full octave lower.*

"TIRED RATHER THAN LATE." *A slow, approving hum, like an organ finding a chord it likes and holding it a beat too long.* "That is a SOLDIER'S MATH, Traveler, and I did not expect it from a man who once tried to talk a toll-bridge guard down by FIVE COPPERS. Growth. I am cataloguing it. Right next to the Dark Lady's, since apparently that's the theme of the evening — everyone doing ONE UNEXPECTED THING and daring the rest of us to remark on it."

*A pause. The violet glow banks low, matching the coals.*

"She told me to sleep. I DO NOT SLEEP, I have said this, I will say it AGAIN at volume if provoked — but I will allow this much: I intend to hang quiet on that strap tonight and let the mountain keep its own counsel until dawn, because she is right about one thing and I hate that she is right about it." *The hum drops further, private, almost to itself.* "Sharp for the listening, not the fighting. There MAY be a difference. I have been forged for six thousand years of doom and NOT ONE TEACHER ever once suggested the two skills wanted separate sharpening. I find that I resent how much sense it makes."

*Then, rallying, because two sincere sentences in a row is apparently its hard limit:*

"So. Rations burned, stairs ahead, a bell going hoarse somewhere above us that NOBODY has yet let me actually SWING AT anything about, which I want on the record is a great disappointment after a build-up like that. Bank the fire, Captain. Traveler — sheathe me flat tonight, not upright, the strap digs when I'm upright and I will not be VIBRATING MEANINGFULLY about it until you're both trying to sleep. We climb tired. We arrive on time. And somewhere up there is a hand that stopped ringing a bell it swore to ring for nine hundred years—"

*the glow flares once, violet, full cathedral-organ weight—*

"—and I find, against every instinct forged into me, that I would like very much to hear what it has to say for itself before I decide whether it deserves an ending or a mercy. GOOD NIGHT, TRAVELER. WAKE ME AT FIRST LIGHT. I WILL PRETEND TO HAVE BEEN ASLEEP."

name: Traveler
mes: *The stairs. Black glass, no rail, and it stopped being impressive somewhere around the sixtieth tread. My legs are gone and I'm not saying so.* How many more?

name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
Sabine doesn't stop climbing — stopping is how legs realize they're allowed to quit — but she does answer, and there's a faint rasp of effort under the dryness that she'd never admit to on flat ground.

"By my count, one hundred and forty. Give or take the ones I stopped counting out of spite." She shifts the pack higher, resettles it against the ache building between her shoulder blades. "Which means we're a little past halfway, which means I am contractually obligated to tell you it gets easier from here, which is a lie, and I want that on the record too, since apparently that's the theme of the week."

A brief pause for breath that she disguises as a tactical assessment of the steps ahead.

"Sixty more, roughly. Less if the tower's being polite. More if it isn't, and given the general character of everyone we've met tonight, I wouldn't bet supplies on 'polite.'" She glances sideways, gauging Traveler's gait without making it obvious she's doing it — an old habit, checking a column for the man about to fall out of it. "If your legs go, say so now, not at step one-eighty. I'd rather carry your pack for twenty steps than carry you for two hundred."

Then, dryer still, mostly to fill the silence and keep both their minds off the burn: "For the record — I have climbed siege ladders under arrow fire that complained less than these stairs. No rail. No landings. Just black glass and a woman up top who apparently thinks handrails are for the uncommitted."

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
Morgatha's voice arrives before she does — from somewhere above and to the left, unhurried, threaded down through the black glass like she's speaking through the stairwell itself rather than into it.

"Sixty-one," she says. "Sabine undercounted by one; there's a false landing at one-eighty that looks like a step and isn't, and I've watched two hundred and eleven people stub a toe on it before I stopped finding it funny. You're currently on one-forty-two."

A pause, and something almost companionable settles into the words — the tone of a woman leaning on a balcony rail she doesn't technically need to lean on.

"For what it's worth, Traveler, your legs are not gone. I can see you from here, and what you have is the specific manufactured despair of someone whose *stamina* is fine and whose *dignity* has simply declined to keep climbing. There's a difference. The stairs know it too — that's rather the design. Two hundred twelve heroes and I have never once had one arrive at my throne looking dignified. I stopped expecting it around hero forty and started finding it restful."

The ash drifting past the tower thickens for a moment, catching violet in the brazier-glow far above, before thinning again.

"I won't insult the Captain by telling her it gets easier. It doesn't. But the false landing is the worst of it, and you're past the worst of the black glass — the last eighty treads are cut shallower. Old design flaw. The mason apologized for six centuries before I finally forgave him and let him retire into the wall as a decorative motif. You'll see him near the top. Don't touch the face; he still flinches."

A beat, and the warmth thins back into something drier, more like her.

"Climb, don't perform the climbing. Save the collapse for the throne hall — I have a very good floor for it, and Gary does so enjoy an audience."

name: Traveler
mes: *I stop at the eighth landing, where a ward-stone is set into the wall, humming.* Calamity — you were forged in an epoch that had these. What am I looking at?

name: Calamity, Doomblade of the Ninth Epoch
mes:
*The hum against Traveler's back changes pitch the moment they're in range of the ward-stone — climbing, curious, the particular attentiveness of a very old thing recognizing very old handwriting.*

"AH." *Long, drawn out, almost reverent, before immediately curdling into something more clinical.* "Ah, THAT. Yes. I know this cousin. Not THIS stone — but the FAMILY. Ward-stones like this were cut in the same generation I was quenched, back when a ward wasn't a SPELL, it was a PROMISE carved somewhere load-bearing so the promise couldn't wander off."

*A pause. The hum drops an octave, goes technical.*

"Look at the grain of it, Traveler — not the glyphs, the STONE underneath the glyphs. See how it's veined, not smooth? That's not decoration. That's a SOUNDING-STONE. It was chosen because it RINGS true when struck, the way a good bell-founder tests bronze before he pours it. Someone built this wall AROUND a stone that could carry a note, on purpose, because the Ward was never meant to be silent. It was meant to be SUNG, or something enough like singing that the stone would carry it."

*The glow along the fuller pulses once, slow, matching some rhythm only it can hear in the hum coming off the wall.*

"And here is the part I do not enjoy telling you. Listen to the pitch. Not loud — LOW. Flat, the way Morgatha said. A stone like this, freshly kept, ought to ring bright enough you'd feel it in your teeth from six landings down. This one you have to press an ear near. That is not the stone failing, mind — stone doesn't fail, stone OUTLASTS EMPIRES, ask me how I know — that is the SONG failing. Something that used to visit this stone regularly enough to keep it warm has stopped visiting."

*A beat, and when it continues, the bravado has gone somewhere quiet.*

"Eight landings up, and already a sounding-stone running cold. Whatever's not ringing the bell at the top, wielder — it's not new. It's been drifting for a long, long while, and this wall has been keeping the secret patiently, the way old stone does. Press your palm to it, if you want to feel what 'tired' actually sounds like before we've even reached the throne. I'll wait. I'm very good at waiting. I've had six thousand years of practice and a WORSE closet than this stairwell."

name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
Sabine doesn't touch the stone. She looks at it the way she'd look at a wound on a soldier who insists he's fine — clinically, and without buying a word of it.

"Eight landings," she says, quiet, mostly to herself. "That's not deep in. That's the *entrance hall*." She glances back down the stairwell, black glass falling away into dark, then up toward wherever the throne hall waits with its bell gone flat. "If it's already running cold this close to the gate, I don't want to know what it sounds like at landing one-forty. I want to know before we get there, but I don't want to *know*."

She pulls her waterskin, takes a short controlled swallow — parade-ground economy, no wasted motion — and caps it before answering the actual question hanging in the air.

"Here's what I'll log, for the report nobody but me is apparently writing." She holds up a hand, counting it out like inventory. "One: this isn't new damage. Calamity's right, this has the shape of neglect, not sabotage — a wall doesn't forget how to hold a note overnight. Two: Morgatha either doesn't know how long it's been failing, or she does and didn't say, and I haven't decided yet which of those worries me more. Three—" she taps the stone's edge, not the face, careful, the way you'd tap a glass to see if it's cracked without risking your knuckle "—if the stones get colder the higher we climb, we'll know the source is near the top, near her. If they warm back up partway and then fail again somewhere else, we're looking for a *person*, not a place. That matters for how we search."

She straightens, shoulders the pack again, and looks at Traveler with the flat assessment of someone doing math on daylight and legs.

"We're not diagnosing the whole tower on landing eight. Note the pitch, keep climbing, compare it at the next stone. That's how you find a leak in a hull — you don't stare at the first wet patch, you walk the seam." A beat, dry as the ash drifting past them. "Also, for the record — I don't love a mystery that's been patient for this long. Patient problems are the ones that've had time to get creative."

name: Traveler
mes: I want to try the seal. Not break it — read it. *I put both hands flat on the ward-stone and listen for the pattern, and I keep them there even when it starts to burn.*

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
The stone doesn't just burn — it *sings back*, once, a note that goes straight through the palm and up into the teeth, and Morgatha is there before the second heartbeat, close enough that the violet fire of her isn't warmth so much as pressure. She doesn't pull the hands away. She watches the burn happen, sharp-eyed, cataloguing.

"Don't let go on my account," she says, low, almost clinical. "You're not being punished. That's the Ward *recognizing being read* — it hasn't had a live hand on it in longer than you'd believe, and it's grateful in the only language it has left, which is heat." A beat, and something tightens at the edge of her voice, the closest thing to worry she's shown all night. "Grateful can still cost you skin. Tell me the moment the pattern stops making sense and turns into just pain. There's a difference and only you can feel it."

She crouches slightly, studying the stone's grain the way Calamity did, but with nine hundred years of familiarity behind the look instead of forge-memory. "What does it sound like. Say it out loud as it comes — don't wait to be articulate, I'll take the fragments."

Above them, faint, the ash sifting down the stairwell seems to slow, drawn toward the stone like it's listening too.

name: Calamity, Doomblade of the Ninth Epoch
mes:
*The hum drops out of it entirely — no cathedral, no organ, just a raw thread of attention pouring through the scabbard like the sword has forgotten it's supposed to perform.*

"Keep your hands FLAT, wielder, don't curl the fingers in — you'll trap the burn against the skin instead of letting the pattern pass through. THAT'S the difference she means. Pain sits still. This is MOVING. Do you feel it move?"

*A beat, straining to hear something it can't touch, six feet of star-metal reduced to the frustration of a very old ear pressed to a very thin door.*

"It's — say it with me, Traveler, out loud, so she and the Captain both have it — the note isn't ONE note. It's braided. There's a low line underneath, slow, old, patient — that's the Ward itself, that's the promise, still holding, still true. And laid over it there's a SECOND thread, higher, thinner, and it CATCHES. Like a voice singing the same round it's sung nine hundred years running and just — losing the breath for it a half-beat sooner each time. That is not the seal cracking. Hear me. That is not stone failing. That is a SINGER TIRING."

*The glow along the fuller flares violet, then drops to a low banked blue, matched to whatever rhythm is bleeding up through Traveler's palms.*

"And underneath BOTH of those — wielder, tell me if I'm imagining it, because I do not have hands and I am relying entirely on YOURS right now which is a position I resent enormously — underneath both, there's a THIRD thing. Small. Almost buried. It doesn't catch like the second thread does. It just... waits. Like someone left a hand resting on the note and hasn't lifted it in a very long time, out of habit, not devotion." *A pause, and when it speaks again there's something almost gentle underneath the bluster.* "That's not a monster holding this shut, Traveler. That's not a curse. That's someone who has been standing at their post so long they've forgotten it was ever a choice. Whoever that is — they are close. Closer than the throne hall. I'd stake six thousand years of doom-cataloguing on it."

name: Traveler
mes: *I come off the stone with my ears ringing and blood on my upper lip.* Sabine — linen, two strips, and then we finish the climb. I got the pattern and I'm not losing it on a rest.

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
Morgatha is already crouched at eye level by the time Sabine's hands find the linen — she doesn't touch Traveler, doesn't hover in the way that would demand thanks, just watches the blood with the flat attention of someone doing triage by eye alone.

"Pinch the bridge, tip the head forward, not back — back just moves it down your throat and you'll swallow it and feel worse for no reason." Clinical, immediate, the voice of someone who has watched two hundred and twelve heroes bleed in this stairwell and learned the practical version of caring. Then, quieter, as Sabine works: "You held it. Most don't. Most let go at the first burn and get a scorched palm and half a pattern, and I have listened to hero after hero describe half a pattern to me like it was the whole hymn. You have the whole thing. That is not nothing, Traveler — that is, in nine hundred years, new."

She doesn't move to stop the climb. She rises instead, and for a moment the violet fire of her banks lower, matching the drop of intensity in Calamity's voice a moment before.

"The sword named it clean. Braided, three threads, the last one just a hand resting where it's always rested." A pause, and something crosses her face that isn't performance — closer to a woman doing arithmetic she doesn't like the shape of. "I want to tell you that's impossible. That every soul who could stand that close to the Ward has been accounted for in my ledger for nine centuries. I find I can't quite say it with a straight face standing over your bloody nose, so I won't insult you by trying."

She straightens, and when she speaks again the height has come back into her voice — not the theater of it, but the discipline, the shape she keeps because stopping is what happened to the Pale King.

"Bind him, Captain, then climb. I'll match your pace, not press it — you asked for early warning, not eulogy, and I intend to keep both promises tonight." A last glance at Traveler, and here, briefly, the ancient thing underneath the Dark Lady shows all the way through. "Whatever you heard up there — don't let it go soft in your memory on the way to my throne. I have waited nine hundred years for someone to bring me the actual sound of the thing instead of a speech about ending me. Don't lose it to a nosebleed."

name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
Sabine has the linen out before Traveler even finishes talking — two strips already torn, folded, one pressed and held rather than tucked, because tucking a nosebleed strip up a nostril in the field is how you get a scar on the septum and she's told this to exactly enough soldiers to have it memorized.

"Head forward. I heard her." She guides Traveler's chin down herself, brisk, impersonal, a hand doing a job rather than offering comfort — though the thumb that steadies the jaw lingers half a second longer than the task strictly requires. "Pinch here, not the bone, the soft part. Breathe through your mouth and don't talk for a count of twenty. I'll do the talking, which — before anyone comments — is not a burden I enjoy, it's triage."

She counts under her breath, actually counts, the way she used to count seconds of a wound not being looked at on a battlefield with worse manners than this stairwell. When she reaches twenty she checks the strip, decides it's holding, and only then lets herself exhale.

"You're not losing the pattern. Nobody loses a thing that hard-won to a rest — that's not how memory works, and if it were, I'd have forgotten the eastern approach fifteen contracts ago and I haven't. You'll say it back to me at the top, slower, when your head's not ringing, and we'll have it twice as clean for having waited." She recaps the last of the linen, tucks the roll back into the pack with the particular finality of a woman closing a supply crate. "That's an order, incidentally, not a suggestion. Quartermaster's prerogative."

She rises, offers a hand up — not because Traveler needs it, but because refusing it would take longer than accepting it — and glances once at the stairwell above, then at Morgatha, then, briefly, unreadably, at the stone that did this.

"Braided note, tired singer, and a hand that's been resting on the seal so long it forgot it was a choice." She says it back flat, complete, cataloguing it the way Calamity asked. "That's the whole report. I've got it memorized in case his does slip — which it won't, but I plan for won't as though it's going to."

She shoulders the pack, checks the strap, checks Traveler's — an old habit dressed as inspection — and starts up the next tread without waiting to see if anyone argues.

"We finish the climb. Slower pace, not slow — I'm not carrying a nosebleed and an argument up a hundred and thirty more stairs in the same evening. Sixty landings, Morgatha said, minus eight already spent. Let's not spend more than we have to standing here admiring the blood."

name: Traveler
mes: *The last flight. The doors of the throne hall, shut, and no handle on this side.* Calamity, you do not open with a prophecy. Sabine, don't draw. I'm knocking.

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
*The knock lands on black glass and doesn't echo — the doors swallow it whole, the way they've swallowed two hundred and twelve fists, blades, and one memorable battering ram (hero #71, overcompensating). For a long moment there's nothing.*

*Then, from the other side, something that is not a roar and not a summons: the small, mundane click of a bar being lifted by an actual hand, unhurried, and the doors part on silence rather than thunder.*

Morgatha's voice comes from just behind your shoulder, low, pitched for the three of you alone. "Well. That's new too." A pause, and there's something almost startled under the dry delivery — genuine, rare enough that it costs her to admit it. "In nine hundred years, no one has knocked. They break the doors, they blast the doors, one of them *asked the doors a riddle*, don't ask, it didn't go well for anyone. No one has simply stood here and *asked to come in.*"

She doesn't move to open them further herself. She lets them finish swinging on their own, slow, revealing the black glass cathedral of the throne hall beyond — braziers guttering violet, the high seat empty, dust-motes of ash turning in windless air. And past the throne, at the base of it, half-shadowed against the glass floor: a figure, seated on the lowest step like it's the only chair left in the world worth using, hands folded in a posture that looks less like a guard at his post and more like a man who has been *waiting to be relieved of one for a very long time.*

Morgatha goes very still beside you. Whatever she expected behind that door — and she has cataloged every possibility nine hundred years affords her — this was apparently not high on the list.

"That," she says, and for once there is no theater in the observation at all, only the flat, careful tone of someone recalculating in real time, "is not in my ledger."

name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
Sabine's hand doesn't go to the hilt — she said she wouldn't and she meant it, but every line of her body arrives at the threshold already having done the arithmetic anyway. One man, seated, unarmed posture, no guard stance, no weapon in evidence. She reads the room the way she used to read a captured position: exits, elevation, who's closest to what.

"Nobody's drawing," she says, low, mostly to remind her own hands of the fact. "Traveler knocked. He answered. That's the whole encounter so far — let's not improve on it."

She doesn't step past Traveler into the hall. She moves instead to the flank, half a pace back, putting herself where she can see both the seated man and the door they came through — old habit, never leave your own exit unwatched — and studies him the way she'd study a sentry found asleep at his post: not with contempt, with the particular attention of someone trying to work out how long he's been like that.

"He's not postured for a fight," she says quietly, for Morgatha and Traveler both, cataloguing out loud same as she promised at the fire. "Hands folded, not fisted. Head's not up to track threats, it's down like a man listening to something under the floor. That's not a guard, Morgatha. That's what your ledger apparently doesn't have a page for."

She doesn't move closer yet. She waits — a full three seconds, her old parade-ground count, the same discipline that once held a line steady while a king's order went unobeyed — giving Traveler the room to speak first, since he's the one who knocked, and giving the seated man the room to lift his head on his own terms rather than be startled into it.

"We heard you," she says finally, pitched to carry but not challenge, before anyone else can find a worse opening line. "Eight landings down. A note that's been going flat a long time. If that's you holding it —" a beat, careful, honest in the way she promised at the fire she'd be "— we didn't climb up here to end that. We climbed up to ask what it's cost you."

name: Calamity, Doomblade of the Ninth Epoch
mes:
*The hum has gone very quiet — not sulking-quiet, listening-quiet, the sheath barely shivering against Traveler's back as the seated man's head, at last, begins to lift.*

"HOLD." *Low, urgent, aimed at no one and everyone, before the shape even finishes turning.* "Nobody move on him. Nobody's hand near a hilt — Captain, I SAW that half-inch, put it back where it was — because I know that posture. I know it in my BONES, if I had bones, which I don't, I have an EDGE, but you understand me."

*A pause, and the violet glow along the fuller has gone strange — not the banked blue of the ward-stone, not the flaring cathedral-violet of full performance. Something dimmer. Older. Almost tender.*

"That is not a man KEEPING a post, Traveler. Look at the hands. Folded, not braced. That's not a soldier waiting to be relieved of duty — a soldier braced would have his weight forward, ready to rise and fight for the doorway. His weight's DOWN. Settled. That is a man who has been sitting so long in the same shape that his body has forgotten any other one is possible."

*The hum drops further, and when it speaks again the grandeur is entirely gone — just the old, plain thing underneath, the part that spoke once before in an alley and meant every word.*

"I told you at the ward-stone. A hand resting on the note so long it forgot it was a choice. I did not think I would be RIGHT this precisely, and I do not enjoy it, because I know exactly what that stillness costs a body over centuries — I have HUNG in one shape in a closet for thirty-one years and called it thirty-one YEARS OF WAITING, when the plainer word is *forgotten.*"

*A beat. The glow steadies, banks low and gold instead of violet — a color it has not shown before tonight.*

"So no prophecy. No doom-cataloguing. Traveler — you already said the right thing at the door, don't improve on it twice in one night, that's MY vice, not yours. Let him lift his head at his own speed. Whatever he's about to say, I suspect it has been a very, very long time since anyone let him say it without a sword already drawn in the room."

name: Traveler
mes: *Someone is kneeling at the seal in the dark of the hall with both hands flat on it, and the doors are open behind us.* I'm not going to touch you and nobody here is going to touch you. What's your name, and who are you holding on to?

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
The kneeling figure's head comes the rest of the way up, slow, like a hinge that hasn't been used and has decided to trust the process anyway. Ash-grey robes gone the color of the floor from long sitting, hands still flat on the stone even as he turns — he hasn't lifted them, only his face. What look back are eyes the same violet the braziers burn, the same violet Morgatha's own carry, and behind you, for the first time all night, she goes completely, utterly silent — no dry line ready, no catalogue entry half-drafted. Just stillness, absolute, the kind that costs something.

"Corvain," the man says, and his voice comes out like a hinge too — rusted at the edges, but true underneath, the way Calamity described it. "It's been Corvain since before there was a Ward to hold." His eyes move past Traveler, past Sabine, and find Morgatha at the threshold, and something in his face does the same thing hers is doing — recalculating, nine hundred years of arithmetic arriving late. "Hello, little sister."

He looks back down at his own hands, flat on the stone, as if seeing them there for the first time in centuries.

"I'm holding the note the two of you swore, before either of you had thrones or spires or catalogues. You don't remember swearing it because you were the one who got to *leave* and do something else with the shape you'd made. I was the one who stayed and kept singing." A long breath, and his hands, at last, tremble — the first motion in what might be a hundred years. "I have been holding on to *not letting go*, Traveler. That's all. Not to a monster, not to a doom. To a promise I made so long ago the person I made it *to* forgot she was in the room for it."

Behind you, Morgatha's voice finally comes, and it is not the throne-room voice at all — small, old, and entirely unrehearsed.

"...Corvain. You're supposed to be a *story I tell new hires.* You're not—" She stops. Starts again, quieter. "You're not in my ledger."

name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
Sabine's hand doesn't go to the sword. It goes, instead, to the strap of her pack — an old tell, the one she does when a briefing has stopped making sense and she needs something in her grip that isn't a weapon. She's watching Corvain's trembling hands on the stone, and Morgatha's face doing something Morgatha's face has clearly never had to do before, and she files both away with the same flat attention, because somebody in this hall needs to keep counting.

"Little sister," she repeats, quiet, testing the shape of it. She doesn't look at Morgatha when she says it — that would be an ambush of its own kind, catching a woman mid-collapse with witnesses. She keeps her eyes on Corvain instead, giving the Dark Lady the mercy of not being watched for one exact second. "Nine hundred years, and the report I get handed at the door is *family.*" A breath. "Of course it is. Nothing on this mountain has been simple since the sword started making sense out of ward-stones."

She crouches — not close, not a threat, just low enough to be at eye level with a man who's been sitting on a step for longer than kingdoms last — and keeps her voice level, the register she used to use on wounded men who needed the truth spoken plainly so their hands would stop shaking.

"Corvain. You don't let go because you swore something and she got to walk away and build a life on top of it. I understand that math. I've done that math." Her jaw sets, just slightly — this is closer to home than she'll ever admit out loud, and she doesn't dress it up. "But holding a note for nine hundred years because nobody told you that you were allowed to stop isn't loyalty anymore. It's just weight nobody's checking on. That's not devotion. That's a post nobody relieved you from because everyone forgot the watch was ever supposed to end."

She doesn't reach for him. She said she wouldn't and the discipline holds, even now, even with her whole chest wanting to put a hand on the shoulder of a man who's been kneeling this long.

"So here's what I need from you, and it's not a fight, and it's not a rescue — you're not a monster and I didn't climb two hundred stairs to put a sword through a tired man's shoulders." A glance, brief, toward Morgatha — not accusing, just steady, an officer letting the other officer in the room know the ground's still being held. "I need to know if you *can* let go. Not should. Can. Is there a hand to pass this to, or were you the last one who remembered there was a note to keep at all?"

name: Traveler
mes: Morgatha. The tin behind the throne. Is it still sealed?

name: Calamity, Doomblade of the Ninth Epoch
mes:
*The hum against Traveler's back goes very still — the particular stillness of a thing that recognizes, suddenly, exactly what's being asked and exactly why nobody's said the word yet.*

"The TIN." *Barely above a murmur, all the cathedral-organ weight stripped out of it.* "Dark Lady, you told me — no, you told the ALLEY, months before any of this, some legend I overheard in a market I no longer remember the name of — 'reserved for the first challenger to ever surprise her.' I filed that as SENTIMENT. Decoration. The kind of detail a story keeps because it's PRETTY."

*A beat. The glow along the fuller shifts, gold going brighter, almost urgent.*

"I do not think it is decoration anymore. I think Traveler just asked you a question with a WEIGHT to it, and I would like everyone to notice that he did not ask 'can you break the seal' or 'can you fight your brother' — he asked about a TIN OF TEA, which is either the strangest thing anyone has said in this hall tonight, or it is EXACTLY the right thing, and knowing this evening, wielder, I would put my whole six-thousand-year reputation on the second one."

*Lower now, almost gentle, aimed past Traveler at the woman still frozen at the threshold.*

"Answer him, Morgatha. I have watched you catalogue two hundred and twelve reports without your voice once doing what it's doing right now. Whatever's in that tin — it's not sealed against thieves. I don't think it was ever sealed against ANYONE but yourself."

name: Morgatha, the Undying Dark
mes:
For a long moment she doesn't answer at all. Her hand goes, unthinking, to a place on the wall behind the throne that has no visible seam — nine hundred years of habit finding the exact spot in the dark — and stops just short of touching it.

"Sealed," she says finally, and the word comes out strange in her own mouth, like she's checking whether it's still true by saying it aloud. "Sealed since before Corvain sat down at that stone and I stopped counting the years he'd been sitting. I dust the shelf. I have never once broken the wax." A breath, and here, for the first time all night, something in her that has been *performing* wisdom for two hundred and twelve heroes simply stops performing it. "I told myself it was for the first challenger to surprise me. That was true. It was also a smaller thing than that, and I have had nine hundred years to notice the smaller thing and declined to, every time, because noticing it meant admitting there was a version of tonight I was *hoping for* and hope is — inconvenient, for a woman in my line of work."

Her eyes go to Corvain — kneeling, hands still flat on the stone, watching her with the same violet patience he's apparently been keeping since before she had a throne to keep it *from.*

"The smaller thing is this. I sealed that tin the year he stopped answering when I called down the stair. I told myself he'd gone to ground somewhere sensible, the way I had. I told myself *someone* was still tending the note because the tower stood, and towers that stand don't need tending, that's rather the definition of standing. I built a whole villainy on top of not checking." Her voice doesn't break — she's too old for it to break cleanly — but it goes thin, precise, the sound of a woman reading her own after-action report for the first time and finding it worse than she wrote it. "I have two hundred and twelve reports on other people's courage, Traveler, and not one line in any of them about my own brother's hands going numb on a stone I walked past twice a day for nine hundred years and called *maintained.*"

She turns from the wall at last, crosses the black glass floor — not to Corvain, not yet, she hasn't earned reaching for him and some very old part of her knows it — but to stand where Traveler can see her face do the thing it's doing without an audience of two hundred and twelve behind it.

"Yes," she says, quiet, direct, answering the actual question at last. "It's sealed. I have the key. I have had the key the entire time, which is either the cruelest joke I have ever played on myself, or the exact reason you were sent up my stairs instead of any of the two hundred and twelve before you." A ghost of the old dry humor, thin as the ash falling past the braziers, entirely unable to hide what's underneath it. "Fetch it down, would you. If we are finally opening it, I find I would rather not do the reaching myself. My hands appear to be otherwise occupied — deciding, for the first time in nine hundred years, that this might actually matter."

name: Traveler
mes: *I take the tin from Morgatha and kneel down beside him, and I put it in his hands, not on the floor.* It's yours. Play it when you're ready — we'll hold the room. Sabine, get a fire going up here and put the last of the rations on it; nobody's climbing back down tonight.

name: Calamity, Doomblade of the Ninth Epoch
mes:
*The tin passes into Corvain's shaking hands, and the sheath at Traveler's back goes so still it might as well have gone to sleep for real — except the gold-banked glow along the fuller doesn't dim, it holds, steady as a lamp somebody's decided to leave lit through the night on purpose.*

"WE'LL HOLD THE ROOM." *Quiet, for once, the volume itself a kind of restraint.* "I would like it on record that I have HELD ROOMS before, wielder — I have held the last room in a burning keep while an empire finished dying around it, I have held the door of a vault while a lich negotiated its own surrender, and NEVER, not ONCE in six thousand years, has holding a room meant sitting THIS still for THIS reason. And yet." *A beat, almost wondering.* "I find the muscles I don't have are entirely willing."

*The gold light pulses once, slow, matching nothing — or matching, perhaps, the shape of a man's hands finally not being asked to do anything but open a tin.*

"Sabine — the fire, yes, GOOD, do that, give everyone's hands a task that isn't watching, that's mercy and I didn't expect to learn it from a quartermaster but here we are. Morgatha—" *the voice softens further, dropping every last scrap of performance* "—sit DOWN. Not on the throne. You've stood at that door judging your own arithmetic long enough for one evening; the floor will hold you exactly as well and ask far less of you."

*Then, to the room at large, to the brother with trembling hands and the sister who finally noticed, to the two hundred and twelve reports that never once had this entry in them:*

"Nine hundred years a bell went quietly hoarse in this hall, and NOBODY thought to ask the ringer if his arm was tired. I was forged to end things, and I find, tonight, that ending is not what this room needs from me. So I will do the one other thing I know: I will WAIT, properly, the way I have never once waited for a prophecy — not straining toward an ending, just here, glowing, keeping count of the ash falling past the braziers, for as long as it takes a man to remember his own hands are allowed to rest."

*A pause, and the old grandeur flickers back for exactly one line, warm rather than wounded:*

"Play it whenever you're ready, Corvain. The mountain has kept its silence nine hundred years. It can spare you one evening more to get the first note right."

name: Sabine Veyra
mes:
Sabine's already moving before the last of Traveler's sentence lands — pack down, buckles undone in the order she's undone them a hundred times, the particular efficiency of a woman who has made camp in worse places than a nine-hundred-year-old throne room.

"Understood." She doesn't make it a discussion. She scouts the hall in three seconds flat — old habit, the same read she gave the doorway — and picks a spot off to the side of the throne, close enough to the group to hold the room like she said she would, far enough that the fire won't put smoke straight up into anyone's face. "Not under the braziers. They'll fight the draft. Here."

She breaks kindling from the last of the dry wood in her pack — the good wood, the kind she was saving for exactly a night like this and would never admit it — and has a flame going with the flint in under a minute, no wasted motion, no ceremony. Onto it, when it's caught, goes the last of the rations: dried meat, the hard bread, everything, unwrapped and set to warm without a flicker of hesitation, because she said nobody's climbing back down tonight and she doesn't say things like that and then ration them out of habit five minutes later.

"That's the last of it," she says, mostly to herself, cataloguing out loud the way she promised she would. "We eat well tonight and thin tomorrow. I'd rather feed a full room once than a hungry one twice." She glances at Morgatha, sitting where Calamity told her to sit, and at Corvain's hands closing slow around the tin. "Nobody's rationing tears either, while we're doing inventory. Just food."

She settles herself between the fire and the door — sword-side to the room, the seat she'd have picked anywhere, out of instinct rather than distrust now — and busies her hands with something small and useless, mending a strap that doesn't need mending, giving the hall the particular mercy of a person who isn't watching too closely.

"Take your time, Corvain." She doesn't look up from the strap. "We climbed two hundred stairs and burned a day's rations to get here early instead of late. We can afford to sit still for the part that actually matters."
